native_result.query: What types of plant introductions were influenced by urban land use?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use in Barcelona province was associated with unintentional plant introductions (accidental arrivals via seed contamination, trade and tourism) and, secondarily and more weakly, with gardening (ornamental) introductions, while agriculture/forestry introductions were not influenced by urban land. Evidence: per-pathway presence/absence logistic models across 632 plots (adjusted for cropland, elevation, road/stream distance, climate, radiation) show Unintentional presence odds rise ~26x per unit urban cover in the 1-km buffer (p<0.0001, also p<0.0001 for 1956-2009 urbanization, ~1.4x per +10pp), Gardening follows the same positive direction but weaker (OR 2.5, p=0.15), AgriForest shows no urban association (OR=0.2, p=0.3); the Unintentional-vs-AgriForest slope contrast is significant (z=2.9, p=0.004) and is replicated at the 50-m buffer. Temporally, Gardening rose to 75.2% of 1985-2019 introductions (chi2=230, p<0.0001) - the urbanization era - while AgriForest collapsed, corroborating which pathway types track urban land. Association, not causation.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected all four files: plot file (632x37, no missing, n.total=sum of pathway counts, 441/632 zero plots) is the only file pairing pathway counts with urban land; species traits/phylogeny cannot join plots (no species IDs in plot file). 2) Primary unit=632 plots; outcomes=presence of n.unint/n.gard/n.agfo/n.total; exposures=urban cover 2009 and delta-urban 1956-2009 (1000m primary, 50m sensitivity); controls=cropland, elevation, road/stream distance, temperature, rainfall, radiation (z-standardized); habitat excluded (proxy/exposure bad-control, reported diagnostically via Firth). 3) Single-exposure marginal adjusted logistic models per pathway (all converged), effect sizes with CIs, per-10pp ORs, cross-pathway slope contrasts (unint vs agfo, gard vs agfo, unint vs gard). 4) Zero-inflation handled via logistic primary; negative-binomial counts corroborate direction; zero fraction vs NB expectation reported. 5) Temporal corroboration via period x pathway chi-square and standardized residuals. 6) Synthesized single natural-language hypothesis naming the pathway types influenced by urban land use.

sub_hypo.relations: Introduction frequencies varied by period and pathway: gardening accounted for 75.2% of introductions in 1985–2019, while agriculture/forestry introductions collapsed. native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use positively and differentially affected introduced-plant invasion by introduction pathway: it disproportionately favored Unintentional introductions (accidental seed/trade/tourism imports) and, secondarily, Gardening introductions (ornamental/medicinal escapes), while AgriForest introductions were essentially unaffected. Per +1 SD (+22.6 pp) of 2009/500m urban cover: Unintentional invaded-species counts +66% (IRR 1.66, p<0.001; presence OR 2.16), Gardening +25% (IRR 1.25, p=0.043; OR 1.49), AgriForest no effect (IRR 0.93, n.s.). Associational (observational), largely carried by urban habitat/landscape placement; AgriForest conclusion is low-powered.

native_result.query: For which domains do the effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB: Original-study effect sizes are larger than replication-study effect sizes in every domain (Social, Cognitive, Economics), with original > replication in 82-88% of paired studies and significantly positive within-domain paired gaps (all p<0.001). The degree differs by domain: strongest in Social psychology (Psychology/RPP project, n=34) where replication magnitudes shrink to ~22% of original (original ~4.5x larger; median |rr|/ro=0.224; 10/34 direction reversals; shrinkage significantly larger than Economics, p=0.003), intermediate in Cognitive psychology (Psychology/RPP project, n=34; ~1.5x larger; median |rr|/ro=0.671; largest median absolute Fisher-z gap 0.249 only because original effects are largest in absolute terms), and weakest/most faithful in Economics = Experimental Economics project (n=18; original ~1.4x larger; median |rr|/ro=0.698; smallest median Fisher-z gap 0.143; only 3/18 reversals). Ranking by magnitude shrinkage: Social >> Cognitive = Economics; by median absolute Fisher-z gap: Cognitive = Social > Economics. Cross-domain signed-gap differences are not significant (ANOVA p=0.75); only proportional magnitude shrinkage differs significantly (Social vs Economics p=0.003). Sign-handling: signed rr (reversed replications count as smaller); magnitude interpretation gives the same ranking. Confound: economics = ee project; social+cognitive = rpp/Psychology project. P0||G0.HypoB: Among black NLSY79 respondents, being jailed sometime in 1985-1994 (ever_jailed=1) is associated with lower composite_wealth at 1985, 1990, and 1996 than never-jailed black respondents, with the gap widening over time (1996 medians: $0 vs $5,000; 1990: $0 vs $3,235). Since no income variable exists, income level is proxied by terciles of composite_wealth_1985; the negative association holds within every tercile (High tercile 1996 median $26,750 vs $4,700; all within-tercile Wilcoxon p<0.001). Controlling composite_wealth_1985 and sex, ever_jailed is negatively associated with 1996 wealth (coef ~ -$42,714, p=0.0008) and 1990 wealth (-$15,356 raw, p=0.13; -$16,464 winsorized, p<0.001). These are associations, not causal effects: jail isn't random, 1985 may overlap the jail window, and the jailed black sample is small (n=159), so selection/reverse causation cannot be ruled out.
P0||G0.WorkflowB: 1) Load CSV (12013x6, no missing). 2) Descriptives by race/sex/ever_jailed. 3) Black-subgroup means/medians ever vs never per snapshot + Mann-Whitney. 4) Proxy income via 1985-wealth terciles (Low/Mid/High), within-tercile means/medians/gaps/n + tests. 5) OLS of 1990 and 1996 wealth on ever_jailed controlling 1985 wealth and sex, with 99th-percentile winsorized robustness.

## Final hypothesis (data-grounded)

**For BOTH white men and white women, wealth inequality was already extremely high in 1990 and was essentially unchanged by 1996 at the level of the standard summary index — yet the wealth distribution shifted shape: average wealth rose strongly (top tail grew), the share of records at zero wealth jumped, and the female-favoring gender wealth gap closed.**

### What moved vs. what did not (white males)
- **Did NOT change — Gini:** 0.792 (1990) → 0.797 (1996); delta +0.005, bootstrap 95% CI [−0.015, +0.026]. Top-10% wealth share flat at 0.621→0.620.
- **Mean rose** 88,163 → 131,792 (+49.5%); conditional on positive wealth, the median doubled 48,100 → 131,500.
- **Zero-wealth share rose** 25.7% → 43.3%.
- **Median fell in the as-supplied sample** 15,601 → 8,900 (−43%) with p90/p50 tripling 13.8 → 37.5 — **but this is NOT robust**: 40% of 1996-zero male-adjacent records are duplicated values and the exact (0,0,0) white row appears 1,096 times (every all-zero row in the file is a duplicated block). After dedup the median is flat-to-up: 31,600 → 37,100 (+17%), p90/p50 rises only 7.8 → 10.6.

### What moved vs. what did not (white females)
- **Did NOT change — Gini:** 0.776 (1990) → 0.782 (1996); delta +0.006, CI [−0.016, +0.028]. Top-10% share flat at 0.592→0.592.
- **Mean rose** 99,605 → 128,837 (+29.3%); positive-wealth median doubled 58,400 → 132,000.
- **Zero-wealth share rose** 20.3% → 42.6%.
- **Median fell in the raw sample** 20,100 → 8,825 (−56%), p90/p50 12.1→37.6 — **same duplicate artifact**: after dedup the median is flat 37,450 → 37,055 (−1%) and p90/p50 rises modestly 7.1 → 9.8.

### Gender wealth gap (between-group, secondary lens)
- 1990: white females held MORE wealth than white males — F/M mean 1.13, F/M median 1.29.
- 1996: gap ≈ gone — F/M mean 0.98, F/M median 0.99 (mean gap ratio 1996/1990 = 0.87, 95% CI [0.73, 1.02]; median-based closure 1.29→0.99 is decisive directionally).

P2||G0.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
P2||G0.HypoB: Among NLSY79 respondents, the Black advantage in education is inversely related to socioeconomic status: it appears only at the LOW end of the SES distribution and not at middle or high SES, but only for college-entry attainment (HG>=13 by 1979) and only under a composite SES of family income, parental education and family size; it is not detectable for BA completion (cells n<5 everywhere) and inverts to a Black deficit under income-only SES at low SES.

native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: Since the earliest available snapshot (1985), the median family net wealth of white (Non-Black Non-Hispanic) individuals exceeds that of Black and Hispanic individuals in every wealth year observed (1985, 1990, 1996), by a factor that WIDENS from 2.2x to 4.3x vs Black and from 7.0x to 16.6x vs Hispanic; every year the ordering is White > Black > Hispanic, with Hispanic medians lagging due to a large zero/near-zero wealth share.
native_result.WorkflowB: Read nls_raw.csv (12,686x61). Mapped cohort 1=BLACK, 2=HISPANIC, 3=Non-Black Non-Hispanic=WHITE proxy (no explicit white flag exists). Metric = median family net wealth for the three wealth snapshots (1985, 1990, 1996 — the only wealth years present). Missingness = complete-case per year (n reported for every median) with a balanced-panel (all 3 years, n=5,739) robustness run because attrition is differential (White-proxy 52.6% missing in 1996). Negative/debt and zero wealth retained as valid observations (no trimming/floored). Bootstrap 95% CIs for medians. CPI-U sensitivity (1985/1990→1996 dollars) used only for growth-over-time statements; within-year group ratios are inflation-invariant. Unweighted: no weight column exists in the data, so results describe this NLSY79 sample.

The race x SES interaction is not statistically significant (LR p=0.42; Wald p=0.40), so racial differences in the gradient are suggestive (clearest for Black respondents) but not conclusive, limited by very few degree completions among Black (28) and Hispanic (19) respondents.

native_result.WorkflowA:
1. One-hot encode Gender variable into MALE and FEMALE
2. Extract the independent variables ['AGE','INCOME', 'BMI', 'BLACK', 'HISPANIC', 'MALE', 'FEMALE']
3. Add dependent variable (DISSAVED) from the df
4. Add a constant term to the independent variable to account for the intercept term in the logistic regression model.
5. Fit a logistic regression model
native_result.HypoB: Across this 1989 cross-section of NLSY79 respondents aged 24-32, age is modestly but consistently negatively associated with the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in: after adjusting for income, gender, race, and BMI, the predicted probability of dissaving falls from about 25% at age 24 to about 19% at age 32 (roughly a 7 percentage-point decline; odds about 4-5% lower per additional year, OR ~0.95). The association is close to linear; curvature is small and not robust. This is a cross-sectional, between-person conditional association (AGE = 1989), not evidence of causal aging, and is consistent with older respondents in this window being, on average, less likely to draw down savings and more likely to add to savings.

Compare HypoA and HypoB in terms of three aspects: Contexts, Variables, and Relations.         E.g., for the hypothesis "From 1995 to 2009, the number of sandhill cranes around the tundra (Indigilka River) surged by an astounding ~10X":
        * Contexts refer to stratification of the data under which the given hypothesis is True. E.g., "For all women", "From 1995 to 2009".

        ```json
        "query": How does age influence the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in?,
        "HypoA": Younger individuals are more likely to withdraw more money from savings than they had put in and with a negative coefficient between age and withdrawing more than putting into savings (-0.0422).,
        "WorkflowA": 1. One-hot encode Gender variable into MALE and FEMALE
2. Extract the independent variables ['AGE','INCOME', 'BMI', 'BLACK', 'HISPANIC', 'MALE', 'FEMALE']
3. Add dependent variable (DISSAVED) from the df
4. Add a constant term to the independent variable to account for the intercept term in the logistic regression model.
5. Fit a logistic regression model,
        "HypoB": Across this 1989 cross-section of NLSY79 respondents aged 24-32, age is modestly but consistently negatively associated with the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in: after adjusting for income, gender, race, and BMI, the predicted probability of dissaving falls from about 25% at age 24 to about 19% at age 32 (roughly a 7 percentage-point decline; odds about 4-5% lower per additional year, OR ~0.95). The association is close to linear; curvature is small and not robust. This is a cross-sectional, between-person conditional association (AGE = 1989), not evidence of causal aging, and is consistent with older respondents in this window being, on average, less likely to draw down savings and more likely to add to savings.,

Script: analysis/analysis_nls_bmi.py; outputs in analysis/results_nls_bmi.json, analysis/age_curve_table.csv, analysis/nls_bmi_summary.txt.
        }
        ```

native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Higher time preference (impatience), as proxied by 1989 savings behavior, is associated with higher BMI by 1992: each one-step increase on the savings-impatience scale is associated with about +0.20 BMI units (approx. 0.04-0.05 SD, approx. 0.6 kg for a 1.7 m adult) after adjusting for demographics, family background, education, ability, and family income (p ~ 0.002); corroborated by lower 1990 net wealth (top vs bottom quintile -0.9 BMI units) and lower 1981 ASVAB-AR (-0.24 BMI per SD) in the same direction. The association is attenuated by about half after controls, holds for attained BMI (1989 and 1992) but not for 1989->1992 weight gain, and is an associational, temporally-ordered pattern consistent with - but not proof that - increased time preference leads to higher BMI.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded NLSY79 (12,686 x 61). Derived BMI(1989/1992, change) from weight(lb->kg) and height(1985,in). Proxies: 1989 savings direction (primary; linear trend + dummy-coded), 1990 family net wealth (continuous z + quintiles), ASVAB-AR 1981 (z + terciles). OLS with HC1 robust SEs, unadjusted vs core vs extended confounder sets, complete-case with per-model n. Alt outcomes BMI1989 and BMI change 89->92; criminal proxies exploratory. Consolidated results in /workspace/model_summary.csv; main script /workspace/analysis_bmi_timepref.py.

sub_hypo.relations: Positive association between the 1989 savings-impatience scale and attained BMI, derived from weight and 1985 height. Adjustment attenuates the association by about half. Savings behavior is modeled as both a linear trend and dummy-coded categories. The temporally ordered pattern is consistent with, but does not prove, increased time preference leading to higher BMI.

sub_hypo.text: Lower family net wealth in 1990 is associated with higher BMI in 1992, corroborating the savings-impatience association.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 participants with complete data for each model; wealth evaluated as an alternative time-preference proxy using OLS with HC1 robust standard errors and unadjusted, core, and extended confounder sets.
sub_hypo.relations: Inverse association between 1990 family net wealth and 1992 BMI: the top wealth quintile has approximately 0.9 lower BMI units than the bottom quintile. Wealth is analyzed as a standardized continuous variable and in quintiles.

sub_hypo.text: Lower 1981 ASVAB Arithmetic Reasoning scores are associated with higher BMI in 1992, in the same direction as the savings-impatience and wealth findings.

sub_hypo.relations: Inverse association: each one-SD increase in ASVAB Arithmetic Reasoning is associated with approximately 0.24 lower BMI units. Scores are analyzed as standardized continuous values and in terciles.

native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: Pottery Form diversity collapsed and Pottery Decoration diversity increased simultaneously in the 17th century BCE (bin 1700 BCE, i.e. 1700-1601 BCE; CE -1700; c. 3650 calBP). On the transition 1800 BCE -> 1700 BCE, Pottery Form Z fell from +0.74 to -1.13 (delta -1.87, collapse to the global minimum, sustained thereafter) while Pottery Decoration Z rose from -0.48 to +0.97 (delta +1.45) - the only 100-year transition with a simultaneous >=1-SD form collapse and decoration increase, and the first bin where the low-form/elevated-decoration state co-occurs and persists.
native_result.WorkflowB: Load capital.csv (comma decimals fixed; CE=-BCE; calBP=1950+BCE; 39 bins, 100-yr). Drop group/color. Sort ascending in time. First differences dForm=diff(ZKeform), dDec=diff(Zkeverz). Criterion A: same-transition dForm<=-1SD AND dDec>=+1SD -> uniquely 1700 BCE (-1.87/+1.45). Criterion B: bins with ZKeform==global min -1.13 AND Zkeverz>=0.97 -> first 1700 BCE (13 bins to 500 BCE). Criterion C: first bin of sustained simultaneous regime -> 1700 BCE (early EN 4300-4100 BCE excluded: decoration at global min -1.92, 'both low'). Cross-check: time_series raw byte-equal to ZKeform/Zkeverz on 37/37 overlapping bins; annual _inter ramp (0.74->-1.13; -0.48->0.97 across CE -1800..-1700) used only as confirmation. Final: 17th century BCE (1700-1601 BCE), equivalents CE -1700 / c. 3650 calBP.

native_result.query: In the PCA conducted on forms of capital, analyzed in hundred-year time slices, how are the symbolic capital components such as house size, daggers, and hatchets/swords characterized in terms of their values on the first principal component (PC1) and distribution across the second principal component (PC2)?
native_result.HypoA: Symbolic capital components such as house size, the number of daggers, and hatchets/swords are characterized by negative values on the first principal component (PC1) and exhibit a wide distribution of values on the second principal component (PC2). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: In the PCA of twelve forms of capital across the 39 hundred-year time slices (4300–500 BCE), house size, daggers, and hatchets/swords all load positively on PC1 (hatchets/swords +0.30, daggers +0.27, house size +0.23), meaning they covary together with the dominant axis of capital accumulation, though none is the strongest PC1 driver (ranks 5/6/10 of 12). Their distinguishing feature is their distribution across PC2: daggers (+0.07) and hatchets/swords (+0.05) hug the PC1 axis with near-zero PC2 loadings (ranked 10th and 12th), whereas house size loads strongly and positively on PC2 (+0.33, rank 5th, correlation 0.50), so in the PC1–PC2 plane house size is rotated ~40–46° away from daggers and hatchets/swords. House size is therefore the symbolic capital component that spreads along PC2, while daggers and hatchets/swords are essentially PC1-only components.

native_result.query: In what context does the gardening pathway for introducing non-native plants show different prevalence styles across habitat types?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The gardening pathway for introducing non-native plants shows habitat-context-dependent prevalence styles: it is the dominant-but-sparse pathway in semi-natural habitats (broad-leaved/coniferous forests, wetlands, coastal; 54-100% of non-native occurrences, present in nearly every invaded plot, 1.3-1.4 gardening species per invaded plot) where invasions are rare but gardening-dominated; it becomes abundant-but-subordinate to the Unintentional pathway in anthropized habitats (urban 29.8%, croplands 18.5% share; mean 0.83/0.39 gardening vs 1.93/1.63 unintentional species per invaded plot); and its species are tall woody perennials with the narrowest invaded niches (0.449 vs 0.749), while temporally the pathway surged from 16.8% to 75.2% of new introductions across the four periods - a modern, deliberate, structural-invader prevalence style that contrasts with the widespread generalist style of unintentional introductions.
native_result.WorkflowB: Executed analysis.py on the 4 staged assets. (A) Temporal prevalence: 4x3 period x pathway chi-square + shares (temporal_trends). (B) Compositional prevalence: 10x3 habitat x pathway species-occurrence table (invaded_niche n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo summed per habitat, n.total internally verified), chi2_contingency + 200,000-iteration unconditional Monte-Carlo p (sparse-cell robust), Cramer's V, adjusted standardized residuals, per-habitat enrichment vs 0.351 overall share and 1-df chi-square, plus 9x3 sensitivity dropping Rock outcrops. (C) Per-plot intensity/occupancy: mean n.gard and n.unint among invaded plots and gardening occupancy per habitat. (D) Species-level: 77 species after de-duplicating the 4 duplicated=TRUE records; pathway means, Kruskal-Wallis and pairwise Mann-Whitney (Bonferroni x2) on invaded.niche.breadth, habitat.range, n.invaded.plots, AOO, mrt, height, native.niche.breadth; growth-form/dispersal crosstabs. (E) Context model (supporting, descriptive): penalized (ridge) logistic of per-plot gardening presence ~ habitat (reference Urban) + elevation + urban.2009.1000m + cropland.2009.1000m + progressive.1993.2009.50m + log distance-to-road + annual temperature, on all 632 plots and on the 191 invaded plots; penalization used because sparse/zero cells cause quasi-separation in unpenalized ML; coefficients read as directions only. (F) Phylogeny: Newick parsed to verify 77/77 (81/81) species tip coverage; optional Mantel permutation test (9,999 perms) of phylogenetic distance vs |invaded niche breadth difference| among 39 gardening species (r=0.014, p=0.353). Formal PGLS is NOT performed (no R/phylolm in runtime) - trait contrasts are descriptive with the Mantel check as a caveat.

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urbanized and urban-expanding landscapes (high 2009 urban cover at 500 m/1000 m buffers and urban expansion 1956-2009) promoted plant invasion specifically by Unintentional-pathway synanthropic weeds (Erigeron/Conyza, Amaranthus, Symphyotrichum, Sorghum, Xanthium). native_result.query: How did urban land use affect the invasion of different types of introduced plants?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promoted the invasion of introduced plants through two distinct aspects: the current urbanised habitat gradient (marginal presence OR per +1SD current urban cover: total 2.39***, unintentional 2.23***, gardening 1.49***, agri-forestry ~1.0) and, more independently, the historical expansion of urban land 1956-2009 (full-model OR=1.54**, p=0.006, total; OR=1.37*, p=0.021, unintentional), while effects on abundance among invaded plots were nil. The urban signal acted on whether a plot was invaded, was strongest for unintentionally introduced species (short, predominantly annual, broad-niche weeds, the most successful invaders: 2.1x gardening and 3.7x agri-forestry spread after residence-time control), weaker for gardening (woody/perennial ornamentals), and undetectable for agri-forestry trees; overall urbanisation (above all urban expansion) increased invasion chiefly by favouring the establishment of the unintentional ('weedy') and secondarily the horticultural components of the non-native flora.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded 4 datasets. Plot-level (n=632): nested presence-logistic models per pathway (n.total/n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo): m0 urban-only -> m1 +elevation -> m3 +3 habitat groups + cropland + log(distance.road) + rainfall + longitude, predictors z-scored; abundance part = NegativeBinomial/Poisson on invaded-plots subset. Urban tested as current urban.2009 at 50/500/1000m buffers and Delta-urban 1956-2009 (500m), plus landscape-change categories (50m, ref=no.changes). Species-level (n=81): pathway x trait chi2, Kruskal-Wallis on success metrics, NB of invaded plots ~ pathway (ref=Gardening) + residence time (mrt), family-dummy OLS as phylogenetic proxy. Python 3.12/pandas/numpy/scipy/statsmodels; no internet.

The urban signal acted on whether a plot was invaded, was strongest for unintentionally introduced species (short, predominantly annual, broad-niche weeds, the most successful invaders: 2.1x gardening and 3.7x agri-forestry spread after residence-time control), weaker for gardening (woody/perennial ornamentals), and undetectable for agri-forestry trees; overall urbanisation (above all urban expansion) increased invasion chiefly by favouring the establishment of the unintentional ('weedy') and secondarily the horticultural components of the non-native flora.
P0||G0.WorkflowB: Loaded 4 datasets. Plot-level (n=632): nested presence-logistic models per pathway (n.total/n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo): m0 urban-only -> m1 +elevation -> m3 +3 habitat groups + cropland + log(distance.road) + rainfall + longitude, predictors z-scored; abundance part = NegativeBinomial/Poisson on invaded-plots subset. Urban tested as current urban.2009 at 50/500/1000m buffers and Delta-urban 1956-2009 (500m), plus landscape-change categories (50m, ref=no.changes). Species-level (n=81): pathway x trait chi2, Kruskal-Wallis on success metrics, NB of invaded plots ~ pathway (ref=Gardening) + residence time (mrt), family-dummy OLS as phylogenetic proxy. Python 3.12/pandas/numpy/scipy/statsmodels; no internet.

Primary metric fiso - fisr (Fisher-z, signed; all ro>0, negative rr correctly inflate the difference). native_result.query: How does the consideration of academic characteristics alter the effects of Socioeconomic Status and race on BA degree completion?
native_result.HypoA: When academic characteristics are considered, the effect of SES on BA degree completion is reduced and the effect of race is enlarged.
native_result.HypoB:
HYPOTHESIS — How considering academic characteristics alters SES & race effects on BA completion (NLSY79 subset; outcome = years of schooling completed by 1979 as an early-attainment proxy)

"Considering academic characteristics substantially attenuates the estimated effect of family socioeconomic status (SES) on educational attainment and reverses the sign of race effects. Without academic characteristics, a 1-SD increase in a composite SES index (1979 family income, mother's/father's education, professional/managerial father-figure occupation, family size) is associated with ~0.37 SD more schooling (Model B); after adding the ASVAB composite this falls to ~0.17 SD, a 55% attenuation (ASVAB block F=1469, p≈0), and family income, father's education, and occupation each attenuate by 54–84% — indicating that a majority of the SES gradient in schooling operates through academic readiness, with ~65% of the total SES association mediated by test scores (bootstrap CI for indirect effect 0.226–0.256). For race, the raw Black deficit (−0.27 SD vs non-Black/non-Hispanic) is entirely accounted for by family SES (−0.02, n.s.); once academic characteristics are also held constant, Black (+0.05 SD) and particularly Hispanic (+0.25 SD) respondents complete significantly MORE schooling than comparable non-Hispanic white peers — an 'over-performance relative to predicted ability' pattern that is strongest in the upper tail (odds of any college rise to OR≈2.7 for Black and 4.2 for Hispanic after adding ASVAB). The SES gradient is steep among low-ability students (slope 0.27 at ASVAB p10) and near zero among high-ability students (0.06 at p90), while minority advantages persist across the ability distribution (widening with ability for Black students, narrowing for Hispanic students). Adding a measure of school performance (class rank) contributes little beyond ASVAB (SES attenuation 51% vs 55%). Caveats: the only outcome available is attainment by 1979 (cohort aged 14–22), no direct BA-completion variable exists (only n=39 with ≥16 years, too sparse to analyze), and the 1981 ASVAB post-dates the 1979 outcome, so all estimates are associational, not causal."

native_result.HypoB:
## DELIVERABLE — Natural-language hypothesis

**Hypothesis:** From 1985 through 1996, the median family net wealth of white (non-Black, non-Hispanic) NLSY79 cohort members was consistently and substantially higher than that of Black and Hispanic members — and the gap did not merely persist, it **widened sharply** over the period. In 1985 the white median ($3,500) was already 7× the Black median ($500) and 2.2× the Hispanic median ($1,600); by 1996 the white median ($42,600) had grown to **16.6× the Black median ($2,562)** and **4.3× the Hispanic median ($9,800)**. White median wealth grew ~12× from 1985 to 1996, versus ~6× for Hispanic and ~5× for Black respondents, so the racial gap in median wealth widened across every snapshot.

**Key numbers it rests on — median family net wealth, nominal $ (n non-missing):**

| Year | White (n) | Black (n) | Hispanic (n) | W:B ratio | W:H ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | $3,500 (5,774) | $500 (2,631) | $1,600 (1,699) | 7.0× | 2.2× |
| 1990 | $12,972 (5,336) | $1,600 (2,431) | $4,800 (1,528) | 8.1× | 2.7× |
| 1996 | $42,600 (3,557) | $2,562 (2,114) | $9,800 (1,368) | 16.6× | 4.3× |

1985→1996 nominal growth: White **12.2×**, Hispanic **6.1×**, Black **5.1×** (ordering/growth replicated on the balanced all-3-years panel: n=5,739; W 3,800→42,600 = 11.2×, BLK 300→2,400, HISP 1,600→9,075). CPI-aid (1996 dollars): 1985 W $5,104 / B $729 / H $2,333; 1990 $15,572 / $1,921 / $5,762; 1996 as above — the widened-gap conclusion is unchanged in real terms.

**Assumptions & caveats (each ≤2 lines):**
- **Cohort coding:** 1=HISPANIC, 2=BLACK, 3=NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC (white) — evidence-based from the file (group 2 lowest median in every snapshot; group sizes match the real NLSY79 oversample design) and the real NLSY79 R0217800 convention. This **deviates deliberately from the datasets.json schema** (1=BLACK, 2=HISPANIC), whose label order appears reversed; documented as an assumption, not a fact.
- **Population & coverage:** NLSY79 cohort aged 14–22 in 1979 (≈20–38 by 1996) — a young-adult-to-mid-career sample, not the full US age distribution; only three wealth snapshots (1985, 1990, 1996) exist in the file, so "1985 onwards" is represented by these points with no data beyond 1996.
- **Missingness/imputation:** complete-case per group×year, no imputation; 1996 is 44.5% missing overall and 52.6% for the White cell, so the 1996 gap estimate is the least certain.
- **Weights:** unweighted — the file has no survey-weight column (only body-weight columns); within-group medians are valid, but population-representative prevalence is not claimed given Black/Hispanic oversampling.
- **Wealth definition:** negative and zero net wealth included at face value (real debt>asset families are in the medians); 1990/1996 tails are top-coded (~84/141 ties at max), which does not affect medians but is why means are not reported.
- **Dollars:** primary figures are nominal; CPI-deflated figures are provided only as an interpretive aid.

Estimates are unweighted, using non-missing observations within each group and year without imputation, including zero and negative wealth. Primary amounts are nominal dollars; CPI-adjusted amounts are an interpretive check. The hypothesis assumes coding 1=Hispanic, 2=Black, 3=non-Black non-Hispanic (white), deliberately reversing the first two metadata labels. Results concern this cohort, not the full US age distribution. Missingness is substantial in 1996 (44.5% overall and 52.6% for white respondents), making that snapshot least certain. Ordering and growth were also checked in a balanced three-year panel of 5,739 respondents.
sub_hypo.relations: Median wealth was ordered white > Hispanic > Black at every snapshot: respectively $3,500 > $1,600 > $500 in 1985, $12,972 > $4,800 > $1,600 in 1990, and $42,600 > $9,800 > $2,562 in 1996. White-to-Black median ratios rose from 7.0× to 8.1× to 16.6×; white-to-Hispanic ratios rose from 2.2× to 2.7× to 4.3×. From 1985 to 1996, median wealth increased 12.2× for white, 6.1× for Hispanic, and 5.1× for Black respondents, indicating sharply widening absolute and relative gaps. The balanced panel replicated the ordering and growth, and CPI adjustment did not change the widened-gap conclusion.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo:
## DELIVERABLE — Natural-language hypothesis

**Hypothesis:** From 1985 through 1996, the median family net wealth of white (non-Black, non-Hispanic) NLSY79 cohort members was consistently and substantially higher than that of Black and Hispanic members — and the gap did not merely persist, it **widened sharply** over the period. In 1985 the white median ($3,500) was already 7× the Black median ($500) and 2.2× the Hispanic median ($1,600); by 1996 the white median ($42,600) had grown to **16.6× the Black median ($2,562)** and **4.3× the Hispanic median ($9,800)**. White median wealth grew ~12× from 1985 to 1996, versus ~6× for Hispanic and ~5× for Black respondents, so the racial gap in median wealth widened across every snapshot.

**Key numbers it rests on — median family net wealth, nominal $ (n non-missing):**

| Year | White (n) | Black (n) | Hispanic (n) | W:B ratio | W:H ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | $3,500 (5,774) | $500 (2,631) | $1,600 (1,699) | 7.0× | 2.2× |
| 1990 | $12,972 (5,336) | $1,600 (2,431) | $4,800 (1,528) | 8.1× | 2.7× |
| 1996 | $42,600 (3,557) | $2,562 (2,114) | $9,800 (1,368) | 16.6× | 4.3× |

1985→1996 nominal growth: White **12.2×**, Hispanic **6.1×**, Black **5.1×** (ordering/growth replicated on the balanced all-3-years panel: n=5,739; W 3,800→42,600 = 11.2×, BLK 300→2,400, HISP 1,600→9,075). CPI-aid (1996 dollars): 1985 W $5,104 / B $729 / H $2,333; 1990 $15,572 / $1,921 / $5,762; 1996 as above — the widened-gap conclusion is unchanged in real terms.

**Assumptions & caveats (each ≤2 lines):**
- **Cohort coding:** 1=HISPANIC, 2=BLACK, 3=NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC (white) — evidence-based from the file (group 2 lowest median in every snapshot; group sizes match the real NLSY79 oversample design) and the real NLSY79 R0217800 convention. This **deviates deliberately from the datasets.json schema** (1=BLACK, 2=HISPANIC), whose label order appears reversed; documented as an assumption, not a fact.
- **Population & coverage:** NLSY79 cohort aged 14–22 in 1979 (≈20–38 by 1996) — a young-adult-to-mid-career sample, not the full US age distribution; only three wealth snapshots (1985, 1990, 1996) exist in the file, so "1985 onwards" is represented by these points with no data beyond 1996.
- **Missingness/imputation:** complete-case per group×year, no imputation; 1996 is 44.5% missing overall and 52.6% for the White cell, so the 1996 gap estimate is the least certain.
- **Weights:** unweighted — the file has no survey-weight column (only body-weight columns); within-group medians are valid, but population-representative prevalence is not claimed given Black/Hispanic oversampling.
- **Wealth definition:** negative and zero net wealth included at face value (real debt>asset families are in the medians); 1990/1996 tails are top-coded (~84/141 ties at max), which does not affect medians but is why means are not reported.
- **Dollars:** primary figures are nominal; CPI-deflated figures are provided only as an interpretive aid.

**Hypothesis:** From 1985 through 1996, the median family net wealth of white (non-Black, non-Hispanic) NLSY79 cohort members was consistently and substantially higher than that of Black and Hispanic members — and the gap did not merely persist, it **widened sharply** over the period. In 1985 the white median ($3,500) was already 7× the Black median ($500) and 2.2× the Hispanic median ($1,600); by 1996 the white median ($42,600) had grown to **16.6× the Black median ($2,562)** and **4.3× the Hispanic median ($9,800)**. White median wealth grew ~12× from 1985 to 1996, versus ~6× for Hispanic and ~5× for Black respondents, so the racial gap in median wealth widened across every snapshot.

**Key numbers it rests on — median family net wealth, nominal $ (n non-missing):**

| Year | White (n) | Black (n) | Hispanic (n) | W:B ratio | W:H ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | $3,500 (5,774) | $500 (2,631) | $1,600 (1,699) | 7.0× | 2.2× |
| 1990 | $12,972 (5,336) | $1,600 (2,431) | $4,800 (1,528) | 8.1× | 2.7× |
| 1996 | $42,600 (3,557) | $2,562 (2,114) | $9,800 (1,368) | 16.6× | 4.3× |

1985→1996 nominal growth: White **12.2×**, Hispanic **6.1×**, Black **5.1×** (ordering/growth replicated on the balanced all-3-years panel: n=5,739; W 3,800→42,600 = 11.2×, BLK 300→2,400, HISP 1,600→9,075). CPI-aid (1996 dollars): 1985 W $5,104 / B $729 / H $2,333; 1990 $15,572 / $1,921 / $5,762; 1996 as above — the widened-gap conclusion is unchanged in real terms.

This **deviates deliberately from the datasets.json schema** (1=BLACK, 2=HISPANIC), whose label order appears reversed; documented as an assumption, not a fact.
- **Population & coverage:** NLSY79 cohort aged 14–22 in 1979 (≈20–38 by 1996) — a young-adult-to-mid-career sample, not the full US age distribution; only three wealth snapshots (1985, 1990, 1996) exist in the file, so "1985 onwards" is represented by these points with no data beyond 1996.

## Analysis complete — diagnostics and candidate hypothesis

Full executable script: `analysis/nls_ses_analysis.py` (executed; full output in `analysis/results.txt`).

### Model-fit diagnostics
- **Linearity check passed**: continuous-SES interaction (AIC 2117.7) beats SES-tercile interaction (AIC 2129.6); tercile model does not improve fit (LR χ²(3)=−5.9, p=1.0). Linear-in-SES on the logit is adequate; the continuous model is reported.
- **Fit quality is modest (rare event)**: McFadden pseudo-R² 0.026 (additive) → 0.031 (interaction); the outcome is inherently hard to predict. All inferences are OR + 95% CI, not p-values alone.

### Primary moderation evidence (M1: `BA ~ SES(1SD) * SAMPLE_RACE`)
- **Headline chunk test (2-df LR, interaction vs additive): χ² = 9.57, p = 0.0083** → significant effect modification of the SES→BA relation by race. AIC improves 2123.3 → 2117.7. Firth penalized-likelihood robustness: **χ² = 16.07, p = 0.0003** — same direction, stronger.
- Interaction terms (M1, Black reference): SES main effect OR = 2.07 (95% CI 1.47–2.90); SES×White OR = 0.57 (0.39–0.82, p=0.003); SES×Hispanic OR = 0.80 (0.47–1.34, p=0.39).
- **Race-stratified SES ORs (per +1 SD)**: Black **2.07** (1.47–2.90), Hispanic **1.65** (1.11–2.44), White **1.18** (1.02–1.36). Slope-ratio vs White: Black 1.76, Hispanic 1.40.
- **Bootstrap (n=1500) slope-difference**: Black−White +0.55 (95% CI +0.17, +0.91 → excludes 0), Hispanic−White +0.34 (95% CI −0.08, +0.72 → includes 0). So the interaction is driven by the **Black vs White contrast**; the Hispanic vs White contrast is directionally consistent but not significant.

### Level differences (descriptive, as requested)
- Nonparametric BA rate by race × SES tercile: Black 0.44/1.87/2.22%, Hispanic 0.78/1.73/3.08%, White 3.05/3.54/3.81%. White exceeds minority rates at every SES level; the gap is largest at low SES.
- Predicted M1 probabilities: White 2.9% (low SES) → 3.9% (+1SD); Black 0.6% → 2.7%; Hispanic 1.0% → 2.7%. **A White respondent at low SES (~2.9%) has higher completion probability than a Black respondent at high SES (~2.7%).**

### Sensitivities
- **+SEX**: interaction intact (χ²=9.63, p=0.0081). Robust.
- **+ academic resources (ABILITY, PERCENTILE IN CLASS, FAMILY SIZE, SEX)**: interaction attenuates to non-significance (χ²=1.75, p=0.42); SES×White OR moves 0.57→0.76. ABILITY (OR 2.33/SD) and PERCENTILE (OR 1.83/SD) are strong predictors; FAMILY SIZE OR 0.59/person. This is labeled strictly as a sensitivity: it shows the race-differential SES gradient is substantially tied to academic-performance resources (ability/class standing/family size) at schooling — consistent with those lying on the pathway — and does not resolve the confounder-vs-mediator question.

### Power / validity caveats (kept explicit)
- Only 236 completers (2.69%) with cells as small as 4–9 events (Black/Hispanic × tercile) → wide CIs; the Hispanic contrast is underpowered. Absence of evidence for the Hispanic–White slope difference ≠ equality.
- No wave/measurement-year info (early-window NLS interpretation flagged as assumption); no weights; associational estimates only, no causal claim.

---

## CANDIDATE HYPOTHESIS (for your review; not yet submitted)

**Explicit hypothesis (payload.hypothesis):**
> "Racial lines modify the relation between socioeconomic status and BA degree completion, but not in the way raw levels suggest: the SES-to-completion gradient is significantly STEEPER for Black and (directionally) Hispanic respondents than for White respondents. A one-SD increase in SES raises the odds of BA completion by ~2.1-fold for Black respondents (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.47–2.90), ~1.6-fold for Hispanic respondents (OR 1.65, 1.11–2.44), but only ~1.2-fold for White respondents (OR 1.18, 1.02–1.36); the race×SES interaction is significant (LR χ²(2)=9.57, p=0.008; Firth-penalized p=0.0003), driven mainly by the Black–White contrast. Simultaneously, White respondents complete BAs at higher absolute rates than Black or Hispanic respondents at every SES level (low-SES tercile ~3.1% vs ~0.4–0.8%), so the racial-line effects combine: SES matters more for minority completion odds, yet White respondents still complete degrees more often, especially at low SES — meaning SES alone does not explain the racial gap in completion, and the SES effect itself is not race-invariant."

**Workflow (payload.workflow):** Standardized SES (+1 SD), logistic `BA ~ SES*race` with Black reference; 2-df LR chunk test vs additive as headline moderation statistic; race-stratified SES ORs; Firth penalized-likelihood robustness (implemented manually); continuous-vs-tercile linearity check; nonparametric race×SES-tercile table; bootstrap (1500) CIs for slope differences; sensitivity A (+SAMPLE_SEX) and sensitivity B (+ABILITY, PERCENTILE IN CLASS, FAMILY SIZE, SAMPLE_SEX); ORs with 95% CIs throughout; rare-event (236 completers) caveats explicit.

**Final evidence summary (for the answer):** Yes — the SES–BA-completion relation is affected by racial lines: the interaction is statistically significant with the gradient steeper for Black/Hispanic than White, while absolute White completion is higher at all SES levels; results are robust to sex adjustment and to Firth penalization, but attenuate once academic-resource measures (ability, class percentile, family size) are adjusted for — evidence that academic resources underpin much of the differential gradient. Limited to 236 completers, so minority-subgroup contrasts carry wide CIs.

- **+SEX**: interaction intact (χ²=9.63, p=0.0081). Robust.

- Only 236 completers (2.69%) with cells as small as 4–9 events (Black/Hispanic × tercile) → wide CIs; the Hispanic contrast is underpowered. Absence of evidence for the Hispanic–White slope difference ≠ equality.

Result: BDD_Scenarios 2.06% CI[0.52,4.12] and MLCanvas 7.73% CI[4.12,11.86] are the two least-used; both significantly below the next named formats. native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: La diversidad de Forma de Cerámica colapsa y la diversidad de Decoración de Cerámica aumenta simultáneamente en el siglo XVII a.C. (primer bin con el nuevo estado: 1700 BCE / CE=-1700 / calBP=3650), en el horizonte entre el siglo XVIII y el XVII a.C. (entre los bins 1800 y 1700 BCE): la Forma cae de +0.74 a -1.13 y la Decoración sube de -0.48 a +0.97 (y luego +1.53), con niveles sostenidos en los siglos posteriores.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Cruce capital.csv/time_series_data.csv (BCE==-CE, ZKeform==PotteryForm, Zkeverz==PotteryDecoration, calBP=1950-CE). 2) Tabla de bins de 100 años y Deltas entre bins consecutivos (ancla temporal: CE). 3) Criterio: colapso de Forma (dForm<=-1.0) + aumento de Decoración (dDec>=+1.0) en la misma transición, con persistencia >=3 bins -> único bin 1700 BCE (dForm=-1.87, dDec=+1.45). 4) Unicidad y sensibilidad: rejilla laxa y umbrales 0.75sigma/1.0sigma (sd 0.546/0.420) -> siempre solo 1700 BCE. 5) Exclusión de 4000 BCE (ambas suben) y del polen (sin columnas de cerámica).

native_result.query: How were the phases of the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE) characterized in terms of the first principal component in a PCA on the forms of capital analyzed in hundred-year time slices?
native_result.HypoA: During the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE), both phases are primarily associated with negative values on the first principal component (PC1). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: Both the Middle Neolithic (3400–3000 BCE) and the Younger Neolithic (2900–2300 BCE) were characterized by a negative PC1 of the capital PCA (capital composite below its long-run mean): Middle Neolithic mean PC1 ≈ −1.39 ± 0.50 (all 5 slices negative) and Younger Neolithic mean PC1 ≈ −1.13 ± 0.44 (all 7 slices negative), both lying between the strongly negative Early Neolithic (−1.76) and the positive Late Neolithic (+0.33) so that PC1 rises across the Neolithic but flips to positive only after ~2100 BCE; the Middle Neolithic negative PC1 is driven mainly by suppressed social (Monument Count, Copper&Gold) and cultural/pottery capital, while the Younger Neolithic negative PC1 is driven mainly by suppressed economic (Depot, Sickle, Axes&Celt, Monument Size) and cultural/pottery capital with social capital returning to neutral.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Load data/capital.csv (39 hundred-year BCE slices 4300..500); convert comma decimals to floats; drop group/color metadata; confirm 12 Z variables complete (0 NAs) and identical to time_series raw values. 2) Correlation-based PCA: standardize the 12 Z variables across the 39 slices (SVD); fix PC1 sign so sum of loadings > 0 (PC1 = capital composite); report loadings per variable and per capital type (symbolic/social/cultural/economic), eigenvalue (3.64, 30.3% variance) and per-slice PC1 scores. 3) Characterize Middle Neolithic (BCE 3400..3000, 5 slices) and Younger Neolithic (BCE 2900..2300, 7 slices): mean PC1 ± sd vs whole-series baseline (0) and vs EN (4300..3500) and LN (2200..1700); dominant capital types via sum of loading × standardized value per type per phase. 4) Pollen Belau_PC1 kept separate as optional demographic/openness context, clearly labeled. 5) Final candidate = natural-language hypothesis above.

native_result.query: In the PCA conducted on forms of capital, analyzed in hundred-year time slices, how are the symbolic capital components such as house size, daggers, and hatchets/swords characterized in terms of their values on the first principal component (PC1) and distribution across the second principal component (PC2)?
native_result.HypoA: Symbolic capital components such as house size, the number of daggers, and hatchets/swords are characterized by negative values on the first principal component (PC1) and exhibit a wide distribution of values on the second principal component (PC2). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: In the PCA of the twelve forms-of-capital indicators sampled at hundred-year slices (37 centennial points, 4100–500 BCE, standardized), the symbolic-capital components house size, daggers, and hatchets/swords load together with the same sign and comparable moderate magnitude on the same pole of PC1 (house size −0.17, daggers −0.23, hatchets/swords −0.28), sharing it with the wealth/monumental indicators and opposite the pottery pole, i.e. they act as a coherent symbolic/prestige-capital axis. On PC2 they do not cluster but spread into an ordered gradient: house size at the most negative extreme (−0.37), daggers intermediate (−0.20), hatchets/swords closest to zero (−0.14) — ordering house size < daggers < hatchets/swords — within a broad margin of temporal PC2 scores (≈ −3.5 to +2.5), making house size the most distinctive symbolic marker while daggers and hatchets/swords occupy moderate close positions.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Cargué time_series_data.csv y aislé los 37 puntos centenarios (CE −4100…−500) con los 12 valores Z crudos. 2) Estandaricé a varianza unitaria y apliqué PCA por eigendecomposición de la matriz de covarianza (numpy; sklearn no disponible). 3) Extraje varianza explicada, loadings PC1/PC2 y scores temporales PC1/PC2. 4) Chequeo de robustez: PCA sobre las series interpoladas (_inter) bineadas a medias de 100 años (37 bins) y comparé los 12 loadings (r=0.996 en PC1, r=0.978 en PC2) y el comportamiento de las tres simbólicas. 5) Redacté la hipótesis final en lenguaje natural con supuestos declarados.

native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: La prevalencia de plantas no nativas introducidas por jardinería es fuertemente dependiente del tipo de hábitat: máxima en hábitats costeros, humedales, urbanos y riparios (media 0.57-0.79 especies/parcela, 36-50% de parcelas con >=1 especie), intermedia en cultivos (0.22) y prados (0.10), y cercana a cero en bosques de coníferas (0.09), frondosos (0.06), matorrales (0.02) y afloramientos rocosos (0.00); efecto del hábitat significativo (p~1e-27) y persistente tras controlar por elevación y urbanización (p~5e-10 a 1e-10).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Carga de los 4 archivos (CSVs tab-separados; verificación n.total=n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo). 2) Métricas de prevalencia por hábitat: media de n.gard/parcela (primaria), proporción de parcelas con >=1 especie de jardinería y share n.gard/n.total entre parcelas invadidas (n.total>0). 3) Modelos: GLM binomial de P(>=1 sp. jardinería) ~ hábitat (LR=146.9, p=3.8e-27); conteo Poisson (LR=196.1, p=2.2e-37) y negativa-binomial NB2 con alpha estimado (LR=148.4, p=1.9e-27); ZIP por inflación de ceros (inestable, descartado como evidencia). 4) Robustez frente a covariables (elevación, urban.2009.1000m, cropland.2009.1000m): el hábitat sigue siendo significativo (binomial LR=62.1, p=5.2e-10; NB LR=65.6, p=1.1e-10). 5) Contraste de grupos alta vs baja prevalencia (OR=0.07, p=2.5e-18) y correlaciones a nivel hábitat con clima/uso del suelo. 6) Contexto: tendencia temporal de jardinería como vía dominante reciente (75% en 1985-2019), especies de jardinería invasoras clave, y composición filogenética simple (gardening repartida en muchas familias).

native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: En la provincia de Barcelona, la vía Gardening muestra dos estilos de prevalencia opuestos según el tipo de hábitat: (1) estilo alto/difuso y dominante en hábitats antrópicos (Urban, 47.7% de parcelas, OR≈35–47) y ligados al agua/costa (Wetlands 50.0%, Coastal 44.8%, Riparian 36.1%; OR 19–52 vs Scrublands, p<0.001), de baja elevación (OR/metro 0.996, p=0.014), donde Gardening aporta 29.8–55.8% de los registros de no-nativas; y (2) estilo residual/esporádico, casi ausente, en hábitats naturales terrestres (Scrublands 1.9%, Rock outcrops 0.0%, bosques 4.4–6.5%, Meadows 7.7%), donde cuando aparece es la única vía representada pero en muy pocas parcelas/especies. Este contraste contextual se explica por el auge reciente y urbano de la horticultura ornamental (Gardening pasó del 16.8% de las introducciones antes de 1500 al 75.2% en 1985–2019, con 65% de su histórico en ese periodo) y por el perfil de las especies de jardinería (arbustos/árboles y perennes, altura media 6.5 m, nicho invadido estrecho 0.45, pocas parcelas), adaptadas a hábitats antrópicos y húmedos, no a cultivos ni a vegetación natural seca.

sub_hypo.text: En Barcelona, Gardening presenta una prevalencia alta, difusa y dominante en hábitats antrópicos y ligados al agua o la costa, especialmente a baja elevación.
sub_hypo.context: 632 parcelas de la provincia de Barcelona; Urban, Wetlands, Coastal y Riparian, con Scrublands como referencia en la regresión logística. El análisis composicional se restringe a parcelas invadidas.
sub_hypo.relations: La presencia de Gardening (n.gard ≥ 1) alcanza 47.7% en Urban, 50.0% en Wetlands, 44.8% en Coastal y 36.1% en Riparian. Frente a Scrublands, Urban presenta OR≈35–47 y los hábitats ligados al agua/costa OR=19–52 (p<0.001). La presencia disminuye con la elevación (OR/metro=0.996, p=0.014). Gardening aporta 29.8–55.8% de los registros de no-nativas, medidos mediante n.gard/n.total. El modelo ajustado incluye cobertura urbana de 2009 a 1000 m, temperatura y distancias a carretera y río; no se especifican efectos individuales de estos controles.

sub_hypo.text: En los hábitats naturales terrestres de Barcelona, Gardening tiene un estilo residual o esporádico: aparece en muy pocas parcelas y especies, aunque cuando aparece es la única vía representada.
sub_hypo.context: Parcelas de Scrublands, Rock outcrops, bosques y Meadows en la provincia de Barcelona. Rock outcrops se excluye de la regresión logística por separación.
sub_hypo.relations: La prevalencia de Gardening es 1.9% en Scrublands, 0.0% en Rock outcrops, 4.4–6.5% en bosques y 7.7% en Meadows. Cuando está presente, se describe como la única vía representada, pese a su escasa presencia absoluta. Este patrón contrasta con el de los hábitats antrópicos y húmedos; la asociación global entre presencia y hábitat tiene p=1.3e-25, y el GLM binomial de composición en parcelas invadidas presenta LR p=4.6e-8.

sub_hypo.text: El contraste entre hábitats se explica en parte por el auge reciente y urbano de la horticultura ornamental, reflejado en el aumento histórico de las introducciones por Gardening.
sub_hypo.context: Introducciones de flora no nativa en Catalonia, utilizadas como contexto histórico para el patrón observado en Barcelona; comparación entre antes de 1500 y 1985–2019.
sub_hypo.relations: La proporción de introducciones correspondiente a Gardening aumenta del 16.8% antes de 1500 al 75.2% en 1985–2019; este último periodo concentra el 65% de su histórico. sub_hypo.text: El perfil de las especies introducidas por Gardening contribuye a explicar su concentración en hábitats antrópicos y húmedos, y no en cultivos ni en vegetación natural seca.
sub_hypo.context: Especies no nativas que invaden parcelas de la provincia de Barcelona; comparación de rasgos por vía de introducción como contexto del patrón por hábitat.
sub_hypo.relations: Las especies de Gardening se describen como arbustos/árboles y perennes, con altura media de 6.5 m, nicho invadido estrecho de 0.45 y presencia en pocas parcelas. La hipótesis vincula este perfil con adaptación a hábitats antrópicos y húmedos y escasa presencia en cultivos y vegetación natural seca; el workflow utiliza los rasgos por vía como explicación contextual.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: En la provincia de Barcelona, la vía Gardening muestra dos estilos de prevalencia opuestos según el tipo de hábitat: (1) estilo alto/difuso y dominante en hábitats antrópicos (Urban, 47.7% de parcelas, OR≈35–47) y ligados al agua/costa (Wetlands 50.0%, Coastal 44.8%, Riparian 36.1%; OR 19–52 vs Scrublands, p<0.001), de baja elevación (OR/metro 0.996, p=0.014), donde Gardening aporta 29.8–55.8% de los registros de no-nativas; y (2) estilo residual/esporádico, casi ausente, en hábitats naturales terrestres (Scrublands 1.9%, Rock outcrops 0.0%, bosques 4.4–6.5%, Meadows 7.7%), donde cuando aparece es la única vía representada pero en muy pocas parcelas/especies. Este contraste contextual se explica por el auge reciente y urbano de la horticultura ornamental (Gardening pasó del 16.8% de las introducciones antes de 1500 al 75.2% en 1985–2019, con 65% de su histórico en ese periodo) y por el perfil de las especies de jardinería (arbustos/árboles y perennes, altura media 6.5 m, nicho invadido estrecho 0.45, pocas parcelas), adaptadas a hábitats antrópicos y húmedos, no a cultivos ni a vegetación natural seca.

native_result.HypoB: El escenario en el que el uso urbano del suelo promovió un tipo específico de invasión fue la urbanización reciente a escala de paisaje (cobertura urbana de 2009 en buffers de 500-1000 m y su expansión 1956→2009 y 1993→2009); el tipo específico promovido fue la invasión de especies introducidas de forma NO INTENCIONAL (ruderales, mayoritariamente anuales, dispersadas por transporte y comercio), que son además el tipo de invasor más exitoso por especie (parcelas invadidas, área de ocupación 10 km, rango de hábitat y amplitud de nicho invadido), incluso tras controlar por la no-independencia filogenética (PGLS). 'Promover' = asociación observacional consistente, no causalidad.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspección de los 4 insumos (temporal_trends contingency 12x3; invasión_success 81x19; invaded_niche 632x37; árbol Newick de 81 tips = las 81 especies, ultramétrico). 2) Parte A: GLM por parcela (Poisson con errores HC3; sensibilidad NegBinomial) de n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo/n.total contra cobertura urbana estandarizada (3 escalas x 3 años) con cropland emparejado, elevación, clima, distancias y lat/lon; ranking por |z| y AIC; robustez con dummies de hábitat; modelos de expansión (deltas 2009-1956 y 2009-1993); modelo binomial de proporción no-intencional; Moran's I sobre residuos (kNN, 0.044). 3) Parte B: parser Newick propio + matriz VCV -> PGLS con lambda de Pagel estimada (max-verosimilitud) para 5 métricas de éxito (log1p para conteos, log para MRT) con referencia Gardening; sensibilidad controlando forma de crecimiento y excluyendo los 4 registros duplicated=TRUE (77 spp., árbol re-podado). Señal filogenética (lambda) por métrica. 4) Síntesis: hipótesis anclada en los valores medidos, distinguiendo resultados medidos de interpretación.

El efecto opera a escala de gradiente urbano-rural/habitat, se absorve al ajustar por habitat ('Urban' concentra 50% de urbano) y persiste como tendencia positiva en habitats no urbanos; la urbanizacion favorece especies ruderales anuales (no intencionales) y ornamentales lenosas/perennes (jardineria), en linea con el auge de estas vias en el siglo XX.

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use did not act as a simple local gradient of invasion risk; it reshaped the invasion of introduced plants through the habitat it creates and through which TYPES of plants it channels into the region: (1) invasion is concentrated in human-modified habitats (83% of urban plots invaded vs 2-6% of natural scrub/forest); (2) which types are introduced shifted with the urbanization era - Gardening introductions multiplied x22 during modern urbanization and dominate new arrivals, AgriForest stayed flat, Unintentional peaked mid-20th century; (3) the only significant local urban signal after controlling habitat/climate/terrain is HISTORICAL landscape change 1956-2009, which raises gardening-species counts and lowers agri-forestry counts, while static % urban cover is not significant; (4) the most widely spreading types are unintentional annual generalists (highest occupancy and niche breadth), even though gardening species dominate recent introductions; (5) species-level type differences are phylogenetically structured - after correction, pathway/trait identity does not predict success, and the robust predictors are residence time and (confounded) occupancy. Association-level, not causal.
native_result.WorkflowB: A) Plot-level hurdle GLMs (binomial presence + Poisson positive-count, habitat fixed + HC3 SE) with AIC scale/period selection over 3 buffers x 3 years (majority-selected 500m/1956), random-habitat BayesMixedGLM, VIF and zero/overdispersion diagnostics, historical-change complement (50 m only). B) Species-level PGLS (Pagel lambda by ML) from parsed phylogeny + OLS contrast; standardized betas with 95% CI; mrt always covariate and occupancy covariate in niche models; sensitivity excluding 4 duplicated species. C) Chi-square of pathway x introduction period with standardized residuals. Synthesis triangulates the three levels into the hypothesis.

native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB: Las estimaciones del tamaño del efecto en los estudios originales superan sistemáticamente a las de las réplicas en todos los dominios (Social, Cognitive, Economics), con gaps paireados positivos y significativos en cada uno; el gap absoluto es mayor como estimación puntual en Cognitive (+0.249) y menor en Economics (+0.196), pero las diferencias entre dominios no son estadísticamente significativas (KW p≈0.44). En términos relativos la contracción es mínima en Experimental Economics (retiene ~59-66%; 61% réplicas), intermedia en Cognitive (~51-53%) y máxima en Social Psychology (~31-36%; solo 21% réplicas), por lo que según la discrepancia relativa original-vs-réplica el dominio más afectado es Social Psychology, y según el gap absoluto apunta a Cognitive (sin respaldo inferencial).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Carga del CSV (86x60) y verificación de calidad (0 duplicados, 86/86 pares completos, Fisher-z exacto). 2) Cálculo de gaps paireados por estudio (ro-rr, fiso-fisr). 3) Resumen por disciplina (media/mediana, IC bootstrap del gap medio, Wilcoxon/t pareada gap>0) y por proyecto como robustez. 4) Contrastes entre dominios (Kruskal-Wallis, ANOVA, OLS de sensibilidad). 5) Sensibilidad excluyendo 18 réplicas con signo invertido. 6) Redacción de la hipótesis en lenguaje natural con los números por dominio.

native_result.HypoB: Aproximadamente el 45.7% (16 de 35) de los estudios replicados con éxito en el proyecto de replicación de Psicología (Reproducibility Project: Psychology, project=='rpp') fueron llevados a cabo por un equipo cuyo autor más senior era un profesor junior (Assistant Professor o Assistant).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Cargar FILE1 (study_data, 927 filas). 2) Verificar que la columna 'replicated' == (p_value.r<=0.05 y mismo signo del efecto) → 0 discrepancias. 3) Subset Psychology = project=='rpp' (97 pares, sin NaN en replicated; 35 replicados). 4) junior = seniority.r en {Assistant, Assistant Professor} (Researcher excluido: no es rango de profesorado). 5) proporción = 16/35 = 45.7%. 6) Sin filtrar 'drop' (denominador 35). Robustez: incluir Researcher → 20/35=57.1%; excluir drop → 16/31=51.6%.

native_result.query: In which domain did both original and replication studies primarily use student subjects (original: 82.4%, replication: 80.9%)?
native_result.HypoA: In Psychology, both original and replication studies primarily used student subjects (original: 82.4%, replication: 80.9%), but some also included community members (original: 7.4%, replication: 8.8%), anyone (original: 10.3%, replication: 5.9%), or online participants (replication: 4.4%).
native_result.HypoB: In the Social domain (social/personality psychology) both original and replication studies primarily used student subjects: originals ~82% (82.2% across 667 rows with subject data; 84.9% across 73 unique studies) and replications ~79-82% (78.6% by row; 82.2% by unique study), the values matching the cited original 82.4% and replication 80.9%. Cognitive studies only reached ~71-76% student subjects in originals, and Economics (n=18, 94.4-100%) does not match the cited figures.
native_result.WorkflowB: Agregación usada: (a) por fila laboratorio sobre las 927 filas y (b) por estudio único deduplicando por id (141; primera fila), siempre con denominador no nulo para el único NaN (id rpp.154). Tabla resultante por disciplina — por fila: Social o=82.2% r=78.6%; Cognitive o=71.4% r=83.8%; Economics o=94.4% r=100%. Por estudio único: Social o=84.9% r=82.2%; Cognitive o=75.5% r=81.6%; Economics o=94.4% r=100%. Sensibilidad: eliminar filas drop==True y/o aggregated==True no cambia la conclusión (Social sigue siendo el único dominio con ambos % ~80%+; Cognitive ~71-76% en el original; Economics n=18). Las filas drop son artefacto (118 filas, todas Social, con sujetos del original inconsistente) y no se usan como criterio principal. El archivo secundario (replication_success) no tiene columnas de disciplina ni sujetos y no participa. Conclusión: dominio = Social; las cifras citadas 82.4/80.9 caen entre el corte por fila (82.2/78.6) y el de estudio único (84.9/82.2).

sub_hypo.text: In Psychology, both original and replication studies primarily used student subjects (original: 82.4%, replication: 80.9%), but some also included community members (original: 7.4%, replication: 8.8%), anyone (original: 10.3%, replication: 5.9%), or online participants (replication: 4.4%).
sub_hypo.context: Original and replication studies in Psychology.
sub_hypo.relations: Students were the predominant subject type in both original (82.4%) and replication (80.9%) studies. Community members accounted for 7.4% of original and 8.8% of replication studies; anyone accounted for 10.3% of original and 5.9% of replication studies; online participants accounted for 4.4% of replication studies.

sub_hypo.text: Cognitive studies have lower original student-subject proportions than the cited original 82.4%, whereas Economics has substantially higher proportions in both originals and replications; neither matches both cited figures as Social does.
sub_hypo.context: Comparison across disciplines using 927 laboratory rows and 141 unique studies, deduplicated by id using the first row, with non-null denominators. Economics contains 18 studies.
sub_hypo.relations: Cognitive student proportions are 71.4% for originals and 83.8% for replications by row, and 75.5% and 81.6% by unique study. Economics proportions are 94.4% for originals and 100% for replications under both aggregations. Social is the only discipline approximating both cited proportions of 82.4% and 80.9%.

native_result.HypoB: The average length (pages) of original papers in Experimental Economics (~28.0, n=18) is markedly higher than in Psychology (~11.2, n=97); a difference of ~16.8 pages (95% CI [12.9, 20.6]).

**English (submission):**
"Among individuals who were ever incarcerated (1985–1994) in this NLSY79-based sample, median 1985 wealth is sharply lower than among the never-incarcerated — about one-fifth the level ($720 vs $3,600 in raw medians) — and this gap holds for every demographic subgroup. Within the ever-incarcerated group, disparities follow a clear racial/ethnic gradient: White respondents have the highest raw median (≈$2,200), followed by Black (≈$320) and Hispanic (≈$0); there is also a sex gap by which men have far higher median wealth (≈$1,000) than women (≈$0). The raw median is lowest (≈$0, with ≈78–81% of group members holding zero wealth) among incarcerated Hispanic women and Black women, although these specific cells are small (n=9–16) and unreliable; the reliable jailed groups (Black men n=143, Hispanic men n=52, White men n=57) show a White > Black > Hispanic ordering in raw median. When zeros are excluded, the racial medians among the ever-incarcerated converge (≈$4,400–$6,000), indicating that most of the disparity is driven by a higher prevalence of zero wealth among minority and female respondents rather than by smaller positive wealth amounts. The same White > Hispanic/mostly-White advantage pattern appears, with parallel though smaller gaps, in the never-incarcerated reference group."

"Entre quienes alguna vez fueron encarcelados (1985–1994) en esta muestra derivada de NLSY79, la mediana de riqueza de 1985 es marcadamente menor que entre los nunca encarcelados (≈$720 vs. $3,600, ~una quinta parte) y esa brecha se mantiene en todos los subgrupos. Dentro del grupo encarcelado hay un gradiente racial/étnico: los blancos tienen la mayor mediana cruda (≈$2,200), seguidos de negros (≈$320) e hispánicos (≈$0); y una brecha de sexo: los hombres tienen mediana muy superior (≈$1,000) a las mujeres (≈$0). La mediana cruda más baja (≈$0, con ~78–81 % de riqueza en cero) se concentra en mujeres hispánicas y negras encarceladas, aunque esas celdas son pequeñas (n=9–16) y poco fiables; entre los grupos encarcelados fiables (hombres: negros n=143, hispánicos n=52, blancos n=57) el orden es blanco > negro > hispánico. Excluyendo ceros, las medianas raciales convergen (≈$4,400–$6,000), lo que sugiere que la disparidad se debe sobre todo a la mayor prevalencia de riqueza cero entre minorías y mujeres, no a montos positivos menores.   - Por sexo: male 1,000 (n=252) vs. female 0 (n=37).

native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: Individuals with a criminal record (jailed at some point between 1985-1994) had significantly lower wealth than those without in all three measured years: 1985, 1990, and 1996.
native_result.WorkflowB: Two-sided Mann-Whitney U per year (1985, 1990, 1996) comparing ever_jailed=1 vs 0 on composite wealth, retaining negatives and zeros; Bonferroni correction over 3 years (alpha per test ~0.0167); 'significantly lower' = adjusted p<0.05 with lower median and mean in the jailed group. Welch t and robustness regressions (rank and raw wealth ~ ever_jailed + race + sex) reported as complements only.

sub_hypo.text: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
sub_hypo.context: Participants in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort, with wealth measured in 1985, 1990, and 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Individuals jailed between 1985 and 1994 (ever_jailed = 1) have significantly lower composite wealth in each of 1985, 1990, and 1996 than those not jailed during that period (ever_jailed = 0).

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.

sub_hypo.text: Individuals jailed at some point between 1985 and 1994 had significantly lower wealth than those not jailed during that period in each of 1985, 1990, and 1996.
sub_hypo.context: Participants in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort, comparing composite wealth in 1985, 1990, and 1996; negative and zero wealth values are retained.
sub_hypo.relations: In each measured year, ever_jailed=1 is associated with lower median and mean composite wealth than ever_jailed=0, with a two-sided Mann-Whitney U Bonferroni-adjusted p<0.05 across three yearly tests (per-test alpha approximately 0.0167). Welch t tests and regressions of rank and raw wealth on ever_jailed, adjusting for race and sex, are complementary analyses only.

native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: The advantage of Black students in BA degree completion rates is positively related to socioeconomic status (SES) levels: it is absent (even negative) at low and middle SES and emerges only at high SES, rather than offsetting low-SES disadvantage. In this NLSY79 subset (respondents aged 21-22 in 1979 with valid highest-grade data), the strict BA-completion proxy (highest grade >=16) yields only 34 completers with <5 per race×SES cell, too sparse to estimate the gradient on its own; the gradient is therefore supported by the complementary '>=13 grades / any college' proxy agreed as robustness. Under that proxy, Black students complete at equal or lower rates than non-Hispanic whites in the lower two-thirds of family net wealth 1996 (the key SES data point: ~7% vs 15% and ~19% vs 30%, Δ≈-8 to -11 pp), but reach a higher rate in the top wealth tercile (~64% vs 52%, Δ≈+12 pp, OR≈1.6; ordinal race×SES interaction p≈0.06). Hence the Black advantage in BA completion concentrates at high SES. The gradient depends on the SES measure: it is monotonic with adult wealth 1996; confined to mid-level with an origin-SES composite (income 1979 + parental education; inverted-U, categorical interaction p≈0.04); and absent with income measures alone (Black always below whites, with the largest gaps at low/mid income).

native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB:
Hypothesis (data-grounded, within-sample interpretation)

"Across the NLSY79 respondents in this dataset, the median family net wealth of white individuals (proxied by the NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC cohort) was consistently higher than that of Black and Hispanic individuals in every wealth wave from 1985 onwards, and the gap widened over time. In 1985 the white-proxy median was $3,500, compared with $1,600 for Black and $500 for Hispanic individuals — i.e., 2.2× and 7.0× the Black and Hispanic medians, respectively. In 1990 the medians were $12,972 (white-proxy), $4,800 (Black), and $1,600 (Hispanic), i.e., 2.7× and 8.1×. By 1996 the medians were $42,600 (white-proxy), $9,800 (Black), and $2,562.5 (Hispanic), i.e., 4.3× and 16.6×, so Black and Hispanic median wealth had fallen to about 23% and 6% of the white-proxy median. The absolute White–Black gap grew from about $1,900 (1985) to $8,200 (1990) to $32,800 (1996), and the White–Hispanic gap grew from about $3,000 to $11,400 to $40,000. Because the white-proxy median grew roughly 12× from 1985 to 1996 while Black and Hispanic medians grew only about 6× and 5×, both the absolute gap and the ratio widened monotonically across 1985→1990→1996 — the median wealth advantage of white individuals over Black and Hispanic individuals was persistent and increasing from 1985 onwards."

Supporting computed numbers actually used (per-year complete cases, unweighted, medians of family net wealth in USD; all Mann–Whitney tests White-proxy vs each group p<0.001):

| Year | White(proxy) | Black | Hispanic | W−B | W/B | W−H | W/H |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | 3,500 | 1,600 | 500 | +1,900 | 2.19× | +3,000 | 7.00× |
| 1990 | 12,972 | 4,800 | 1,600 | +8,172 | 2.70× | +11,372 | 8.11× |
| 1996 | 42,600 | 9,800 | 2,562.5 | +32,800 | 4.35× | +40,038 | 16.62× |

Within-group median growth 1985→1996: White(proxy) 3,500→12,972→42,600 (12.2×); Black 1,600→4,800→9,800 (6.1×); Hispanic 500→1,600→2,562.5 (5.1×). Bootstrap 95% CIs for the medians do not overlap between groups in any year (e.g., 1996 White 40,750–46,000; Black 8,198–11,550; Hispanic 2,000–3,000).

Key caveats framing this as a within-sample interpretation (not nationally representative totals): (1) "white" is proxied by the NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC cohort label, the closest available category; (2) "from 1985 onwards" = the three available net-wealth waves (1985, 1990, 1996); (3) wealth is family-level, assigned to each individual respondent (one row per person); (4) estimates are unweighted (no survey-weight column in the file; NLSY79 oversampled Black/Hispanic youth); (5) missingness rises over time and is group-imbalanced, most notably in 1996 where 52.6% of NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC respondents lack a wealth value (vs 31.7% Black, 33.4% Hispanic), so later waves describe observed respondents; (6) net wealth includes negative and zero values (retained) and is top-coded at the same ceiling per year across all three groups, which does not affect medians.
